title: Quantization Technical Review - Silverridge AI
summary: Technical deep dive on quantization tradeoffs (GPTQ vs AWQ vs INT8/FP8), observed accuracy regressions on Silverridge's 13B model, runtime implications for KV cache and batching, and on-prem/VPC deployment constraints. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run targeted benchmarks, share quantization runbook + perf profiles, schedule 1-week on-prem pilot.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Time: 14:00 - 14:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SWE), Priya Nair (Silverridge CTO), Daniel Gomez (ML Eng), Sara Li (Infra)

Summary (auto): Quick review of Silverridge's quantization experiments; discussed GPTQ/AWQ/INT8+FP8 tradeoffs, KV cache behavior with quantized weights, batching/prefetch impacts on latency, and constraints for their VPC/on-prem deployment. Action items assigned for benchmarking and security docs.

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, uh, Marcus is gonna lead the tech side.
[00:18] Marcus: hey, hi all. So Priya, Daniel, Sara, nice to meet you. Today we want to go deep on the accuracy regressions you've seen after converting your 13B model to INT8 and GPTQ variants, and figure out a path that balances throughput and quality.
[00:35] Priya: thanks, Marcus. Yeah so we've been testing GPTQ and AWQ on a 13B model derived from Llama2 family, og weight is fine, but after gptq we saw about 3.5-4% drop on our internal NLU suite. fp8 results were closer but the runtime on our infra blew up.
[01:02] Daniel: to add, our typical sequence lengths are 512 tokens for inference, p95 latency target is ~220ms per request, and we need ~60 concurrent qps during peak.
[01:20] Marcus: ok that's helpful. couple clarifying q's: are you using prefix KV cache across calls or stateless requests?
[01:29] Sara: mostly stateless but we do some short multi-turn where we keep the KV cache for 1-3 turns. we tried caching with the gptq model and it hit a memory blow-up on our 80GB gpu nodes.
[01:44] Diego: (inaudible) memory blow-up sounds like mixed-precision kv cache misalignment. sometimes quantized kernels store kv in fp16 and if weights are int8 conversions mismatch can spike memory.
[02:03] Daniel: yes, that's what we see. also, with AWQ we saw slightly better accuracy than GPTQ on some benchmarks but throughput was lower than INT8 ops.
[02:20] Marcus: right. quick primer: INT8 (and INT8 with per-channel calibration) is usually fastest on modern kernels, but can cause larger accuracy drops on some models unless we do selective higher-precision layers. GPTQ is post-training quantization optimized for LLM weights and often preserves accuracy better than naive INT8, but runtime support is spotty: some runtimes accelerate GPTQ well, others not. AWQ is a recent technique that aims to get GPTQ-like quality with more runtime-friendly layouts — but it's implementation dependent.
[02:51] Priya: could you explain the fp8 tradeoff? our infra team saw FP8 improved quality but increased GPU utilization and caused more OOMs.
[03:02] Marcus: FP8 keeps more dynamic range, so accuracy is often better; however FP8 kernels may not be as optimized and can require extra scratch space for accumulation or fallback to fp16 in parts, which increases memory usage. If your KV cache remains in fp16 while weights are fp8 you get mixed-type buffers that cost more.
[03:28] Sara: we ran a test where FP8 reduced our avg latency from 210ms to 190ms for single requests but concurrently the GPU mem utilization jumped and we couldn't sustain the 60 qps.
[03:40] Marcus: that matches expectations; FP8 helps arithmetic but not necessarily the memory profile. we typically recommend selective quantization: keep embedding and first/last n layers in higher precision and quantize the middle layers.
[03:55] Daniel: when you say "selective", how do you profile which layers to keep?
[04:01] Marcus: good question — we run a per-layer sensitivity pass. Redwood's quantization profiler will run a diff on your eval set and produce a ranked list of layers by accuracy sensitivity and memory/latency impact. we'll share that profiler with you.
[04:17] Priya: great. do you have any guidance for KV cache with quantized models? that's where we hit the OOMs.
[04:24] Marcus: kv cache is tricky. two things: 1) layout: some runtimes keep kv in fp16 regardless of weight quantization which doubles mem compared to int8. 2) pre-allocation: if you pre-allocate for max sequence length and concurrency you can run out fast. Our runtime supports dynamic kv allocation and streaming kv where we flush older prefixes for stateless workloads. For on-prem we can tune the allocator to reduce peak.
[04:49] Diego: add to that — if you quantize weights with per-token packing we sometimes see slower KV reads because of extra unpacking steps; AWQ mitigates some unpack cost because it aligns layout for faster matmuls.
[05:08] Priya: what's your recommendation for their particular 13B model and their latency targets (p95 220ms)?
[05:16] Marcus: initial recommendation: run GPTQ and AWQ variants with selective high-precision for first 2 and last 2 layers, measure accuracy on your NLU set, and run a throughput test with realistic batching patterns (we suspect batching will help throughput without violating p95 if you keep batch sizes small). If memory is the blocker, try AWQ+fp16 KV cache to reduce unpack overhead.
[05:41] Daniel: we tried larger batches and latency spiked for tail requests. our traffic is spiky so we can't batch aggressively.
[05:49] Marcus: okay then focus on concurrency scaling — dedicate multiple inference workers (shard by replica) with smaller batch sizes per worker. Redwood Dedicated supports that topology.
[05:59] Sara: how about kernel selection — will Redwood runtime pick best kernels per hardware automatically? we're on A100 and also testing on L40s.
[06:08] Diego: yes, runtime will profile and choose the best kernel paths; on A100 INT8 kernels are well optimized, on L40 FP8 paths may be better. Also for AWQ/GPTQ we have specific fused kernels in our latest runtime build. we need to match CUDA/cuDNN versions; small mismatches can degrade perf.
[06:32] Priya: we run Ubuntu 22.04, driver versions are pretty recent. we'll share exact infra spec after the call.
[06:38] Marcus: please do. quick note on accuracy regressions: you mentioned 3.5-4% drop on NLU. what's the baseline metric?
[06:46] Daniel: baseline is F1 on our intent extraction suite; baseline 92% -> quantized 88.5% on GPTQ (current config). AWQ gave 90.8% but slower.
[07:00] Marcus: ok that magnitude is fixable in many cases with selective higher-precision layers or hybrid quantization (e.g., outlier-aware). we'll propose a profile to test: GPTQ baseline, AWQ baseline, GPTQ plus last-3 layers fp16, AWQ with per-channel calibration.
[07:18] Priya: curious about regression repro: could it be tokenization or perf differences across tokenizers?
[07:24] Marcus: yes tokenizer shifts can cause diffs; ensure you compare inference outputs token-for-token on same checkpoint, same tokenizer, same decoding params. Redwood's bench harness locks those.
[07:36] Daniel: on the runtime side, when we tried to keep kv in int8 we saw mismatched results vs cpu reference by a few tokens. is that expected?
[07:45] Diego: small token diffs can come from numerical differences in matmul accumulation or rounding; if exact determinism is required you need deterministic kernels and consistent accumulation precision. Quantization amplifies these differences.
[07:59] Sara: can Redwood provide a deterministic run to validate?
[08:03] Marcus: yes we can run deterministic seeds and provide bitwise-diff comparisons for a set of test prompts.
[08:10] Priya: perfect. next, on VPC/on-prem constraints — we want to run a pilot in our VPC with customer-managed KMS and strict egress controls. will that impact quantization or runtime?
[08:20] Diego: it won't affect quantization itself, but it impacts how we ship optimized binaries and kernel libs. for air-gapped we provide an on-prem package with prebuilt kernels; you need to match driver stack. KMS doesn't change runtime behavior.
[08:34] Priya: any perf differences between hosted Redwood and on-prem?
[08:39] Marcus: on-prem perf depends on hardware and driver stack; our hosted infra has tuned kernels and the latest low-level libraries. On-prem can match if you pin driver versions and we provide optimized kernel builds.
[08:52] Daniel: question on benchmarking methodology — what workload should we run to mimic our production mix?
[08:58] Marcus: run a mixed workload: 70% stateless single-turn short prompts (avg seq 128), 20% multi-turn avg seq 512 with kv reuse, 10% long-ranging context (1024+). Also simulate your concurrency spikes. We'll provide a harness.
[09:18] Priya: good. one more — about AWQ licensing or IP concerns? we've seen AWQ libs from a few sources.
[09:26] Marcus: AWQ implementations are from community and some vendors; Redwood's runtime integrates AWQ algorithms but the runtime is under Redwood's license. we'll include licensing notes in the runbook.
[09:38] Diego: practical note — AWQ tends to produce slightly larger binary kernels due to pack/unpack code which can affect cold start times.
[09:47] Daniel: that could explain our initial slower first request.
[09:51] Marcus: yep. we can mitigate via warmup jobs.
[09:55] Lena: quick recap — agreed path: Redwood runs three benchmark tracks against your 13B model: GPTQ baseline, AWQ baseline, and hybrid selective-precision. We'll measure accuracy (your NLU suite), latency p50/p95, throughput, and GPU memory. We'll also test kv cache strategies (fp16 vs int8 caching) and small-batch vs sharded workers.
[10:16] Priya: timeline?
[10:19] Marcus: we can start bench runs as soon as you share the model checkpoint and perf infra access (or we can run on a snapshot dataset if you can't share weights). estimate initial results in 5 business days.
[10:31] Sara: on the infra side, we'll need an on-prem build to test L40 FP8 paths; could Redwood provide that?
[10:39] Diego: yes, we'll produce a container with prebuilt kernels for L40 and A100, but we need your exact driver/CUDA versions.
[10:47] Daniel: for the memory blow-ups we saw, any quick hotfix before deeper benching?
[10:52] Marcus: short term: reduce max prefix length pre-allocation, enable streaming kv (evict older tokens), and pin first/last layers to fp16. That should reduce peak memory.
[11:04] Priya: ok. also you're going to share the profiler and quantization runbook, correct?
[11:08] Lena: yes, we'll send the profiler, a runbook with recommended configs for GPTQ/AWQ/INT8, and a sample benchmark harness.
[11:16] (brief cross talk)
[11:23] Marcus: quick technical aside — regarding accuracy metrics, also watch out for outlier tokens. sometimes macro F1 hides tail-case hallucinations; we recommend adding a qualitative prompt set to catch regressions that matter for you.
[11:39] Priya: we'll prep a small set of customer-critical prompts.
[11:42] Diego: last infra note: if you plan to run VPC, we can do the pilot in your VPC with a temporary host access to push the optimized kernels securely.
[11:52] Priya: sounds good.
[11:55] Lena: great. we'll wrap soon, any final q's?
[11:58] Daniel: none here.
[12:00] Sara: no.
[12:02] Lena: ok final recap and next steps...
